# Local resolution weighting

Local resolution weighting (LRW) combines acquisitions pixel by pixel and gives
more weight to the acquisitions that resolve the terrain more finely at that
pixel. s1bursts follows Small et al. (2022)[^small] and applies the method to
backscatter and coherence alike.

## Why mountains need it

A radar looks sideways, so the ground resolution of a mountain slope depends on
how the slope faces the sensor. A slope facing the sensor is compressed into
few pixels and coarsely resolved. A slope facing away is stretched over many
pixels and finely resolved, unless it is so steep that it lies in radar shadow.
Ascending and descending orbits look from opposite sides, so each resolves
slopes that the other resolves poorly.

## The weights

The `scattering_area` band of an RTC product holds the normalized ground area
$A_i$ that acquisition $i$ observes in each pixel. Its inverse is the local
resolution, $r_i = 1/A_i$. At each pixel, the weights are the local
resolutions, normalized to sum to one over the $M$ acquisitions with a valid
observation there:

$$
W_i = \frac{r_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{M} r_j}
$$

The composite of a measured value $x$ is the weighted mean

$$
x_c = \sum_{i=1}^{M} W_i \, x_i ,
$$

or the weighted median or quantile with `aggregation="median"` or a quantile
level. The weights depend only on the viewing geometry, so $x$ can be
backscatter $\gamma^0$ or coherence. A coherence product has no scattering
area of its own, so each pair is weighted by the RTC product of its primary
acquisition, which is why `compose_coherence_lrw()` takes RTC products as
well.

An acquisition in radar shadow has no valid area there and does not count
toward $M$. Bursts of the same orbit and date are joined first, so the overlap
of neighboring bursts counts once.

## Capping the local resolution

Close to radar shadow, $A_i$ approaches zero and $r_i$ grows without bound,
although the simulated area is least reliable there. `clip_max_resolution`
sets a cap $r_\text{max}$ and uses $\min(r_i, r_\text{max})$ in place of $r_i$
in the weights, so that one acquisition cannot dominate such pixels. By
default, no cap is applied. For scale, flat terrain has a local resolution of
about 0.6 to 1.0.

## The quality layers

The number of observations (`QA-NUM`) is $M$, the number of acquisitions that
contributed to each pixel. The composite quality map (`QA-CQM`) is the local
resolution of the composite: the inverse of the mean scattering area, weighted
as the composite is:

$$
\text{CQM} = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{M} W_i \, A_i \right)^{-1}
$$

A higher value means a finer resolution. The quality map describes the viewing
geometry only, not the accuracy of the measured value. With a median or
quantile, it is still the weighted mean above, so it describes the weighting
rather than the acquisitions that supplied each value.

[^small]: Small, D., Rohner, C., Miranda, N., Ruetschi, M., & Schaepman, M. E.
    (2022). Wide-area analysis-ready radar backscatter composites. *IEEE
    Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing*, 60, 5201814.
